temperature.name: Temperature
temperature.question: Is it getting hotter?
temperature.definition: The air temperature about 6 feet above the ground, averaged over day and night: what you feel when you step outside.
temperature.why: Hotter air raises the risk of heat illness, pushes up electricity bills and stresses crops.

rainfall.name: Rain
rainfall.question: Is the rain changing?
rainfall.definition: How much rain falls in a year.
rainfall.why: More rain can mean more flooding. Less rain can mean drought, wildfires and limits on water use.
rainfall.source: NASA MERRA-2 (corrected with rain gauges), via NASA POWER

humidity.name: Humidity
humidity.question: Is it getting muggier?
humidity.up: the air in {place} is getting muggier
humidity.down: the air in {place} is getting less muggy
humidity.definition: How much moisture is in the air, measured by the dew point. The higher the dew point, the stickier it feels: above 65 °F (18 °C) feels sticky, above 70 °F (21 °C) feels oppressive.
humidity.why: Humid air stops sweat from drying, so the body overheats faster. Heat plus humidity is Florida's real danger.

sea_level.name: Sea level
sea_level.question: Is the sea rising?
sea_level.measure: Sea level compared with its 1983–2001 average
sea_level.definition: The average height of the ocean at the coast, measured by a tide gauge. Averaging over a whole month removes the daily tides and waves.
sea_level.why: Higher seas mean more flooding at high tide ('sunny-day flooding'), stronger storm surges and salt water creeping into drinking water wells.
sea_level.source: NOAA tide gauges (NASA uses tide gauge records to check its satellite sea level data)

miami.name: Miami

temperature.up: Greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels trap extra heat: the main long-term cause of warming worldwide. Cities add their own heat (the 'urban heat island'): pavement and buildings soak up sunlight and release it slowly. Natural cycles such as El Niño make some years hotter than others.
temperature.down: Natural cycles such as La Niña, or a large volcanic eruption, can cool a region for a few years. A long cooling trend is unusual today, so double-check the years you picked.

humidity.up: Warmer air can hold more water vapor (about 7% more for each 1 °C, or 4% per °F), and warmer oceans around Florida evaporate more water into the air.
humidity.down: Drier air masses, less evaporation from land, or changes in wind patterns can lower humidity.

rainfall.up: Warmer air holds more water vapor, so heavy rain can get heavier. Changes in tropical storms and sea breezes also change how much rain an area gets.
rainfall.down: Shifting weather patterns can steer storms away from a region. Cycles such as La Niña usually bring drier winters to Florida.

sea_level.up: Two main causes: ocean water expands as it warms, and melting glaciers and ice sheets add water to the ocean. In some places the land is also slowly sinking, which makes the sea rise faster there. Changes in ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream can speed up or slow down the rise along Florida's coasts for years at a time.
sea_level.down: A falling sea level is very unusual today. It can happen where the land is rising, or for a few years when ocean currents shift. Double-check the years you picked.

The basics: A steady change in one direction over a long time: up or down.
The same measurement repeated over time and put in order.
Miami's average temperature for every month since 1981.
Ten years. We report change 'every 10 years' so the numbers are easy to compare.
The pattern that repeats every year, like hot summers and mild winters. We remove it before looking for a trend, so a hot August is only compared with other Augusts.
Is this July warmer than a normal July?
Random ups and downs that are not part of any trend.
One very rainy year does not mean Florida is getting wetter.
The straight line that best follows the data. Its tilt shows the direction and speed of change.
A line tilting up means a rising trend.
How sure are we?: Very unlikely to be caused by luck alone. Scientists usually require less than a 5% chance of luck.
The chance of seeing a trend this strong if nothing were really changing. Smaller means stronger evidence.
p = 0.03 means a 3% chance it is just luck.
Compares every month with every later month. If later months are higher (or lower) far more often than chance allows, there is a trend.
The typical rate of change between all pairs of months. One strange value barely affects it.
A range that very likely contains the true rate of change.
Florida and the data: Dew point
The temperature at which air becomes full of water. A higher dew point means muggier air.
A dew point of 75 °F (24 °C) feels oppressive.
Heat index
What the temperature feels like when humidity is included.
90 °F with high humidity can feel like 105 °F.
Urban heat island
Cities are warmer than the countryside because pavement and buildings store heat.
Downtown Miami vs. the Everglades at night.
Tide gauge
An instrument at the coast that measures the height of the sea every few minutes. Monthly averages remove the tides.
Key West's gauge has measured the sea since 1913.
Relative sea level
Sea level compared with the land next to it. It rises if the ocean rises, or if the land sinks.
What a tide gauge measures, and what matters for flooding.
Sunny-day flooding
Flooding at very high tides, even with no rain or storm.
Streets in Miami Beach flooding during autumn 'king tides'.
El Niño / La Niña
Natural swings in Pacific Ocean temperature that change weather worldwide for a year or two.
El Niño winters are usually wetter in Florida.
MERRA-2
NASA's computer reconstruction of the weather since 1980, built from satellites, weather balloons and ground stations.
Our temperature, rain and humidity data.
NASA POWER
A free NASA service that delivers MERRA-2 data for any point on Earth.
This site downloads Florida data from it.
Resolution
The size of the smallest area the data can show.
MERRA-2 squares are about 50 km (30 miles) wide.
